title: Wind generator from a treadmill motor
summary: Turn a treadmill's permanent-magnet DC motor into a small wind generator that charges a 12V battery. Expect nothing in light wind, tens of watts in a steady breeze and 100–300W in strong wind. The tower is the dangerous part. It must always have a battery and a dump load connected so it never runs unloaded.

materials.item: Treadmill motor: permanent-magnet DC, 90–180V, 1.5–3 hp, with its flywheel
Bridge rectifier 25–35A, 100V or more, on a heatsink (or a Schottky diode of the same rating)
Heatsink for the rectifier and dump-load MOSFET
Deep-cycle 12V battery or bank, 50Ah or more
Fuse and holder near the battery, 30–40A
Cable from turbine to battery, 10–6 AWG (6–16 mm²) depending on distance
Dump load: 12V halogen headlight bulbs or power resistors, about 1.5× the turbine's peak watts
N-channel MOSFET 60V or more, 60A or more (or two in parallel), to switch the dump load
TL431 shunt reference for the dump-load trigger
PNP transistor and small resistors, plus a 10 kΩ trimmer
Heavy toggle switch for the brake (shorts the motor), 30A or more
PVC pipe 150–200 mm diameter, 600–750 mm long, for blades
Steel or aluminium plate 3–6 mm thick, about 250 mm across, for the hub and tail vane
Steel pipe 40–50 mm heavy wall, 6–10 m, for the tower; plus square tube or channel, about 1.5 m, for the head and tail boom
Steel guy cable 4–6 mm with wire-rope clips
Bolts, nuts and lock washers, M6–M10
Bearing or greased pipe sleeve for the yaw joint
Panel ammeter or a clamp meter to watch output

steps.text: Read the motor nameplate. Work out volts per 1,000 rpm: rated volts ÷ rated rpm × 1,000 (130V at 6,700 rpm is about 19). Higher is better: 30 or more starts charging in moderate wind, under 20 only charges in strong wind. Check it spins freely and the brushes are good (test_motor).
Find which way the flywheel screws tighter on its shaft. That is the direction the rotor must turn. Spin the motor that way with a drill and mark which lead goes positive.

Cut the PVC pipe lengthwise into four strips and keep three. Taper each one: keep the full width for the first 100 mm at the root, then cut in a straight line down to about 40–50 mm wide at the tip. Leave one long edge straight; it is the leading edge. Sand all edges smooth.
steps.warn: Clamp the pipe before cutting. Cut edges of PVC are sharp.

steps.text: Mark three lines 120° apart on the hub plate. Bolt each blade flat to the plate with two bolts, hollow side facing the wind and straight edge leading in the turning direction you found. All three tips must sit the same distance from the centre.
Balance the rotor: hang it level on a bolt through the centre hole. If one blade always drops, trim its tip or add a washer to the light blades until it stays wherever you stop it.

Bolt the hub to the flywheel. Mount the motor on the front of the head tube, fit the yaw sleeve (a short pipe that slides over the tower top) just behind the motor, and fix a 1–1.2 m tail boom with a 0.1–0.2 m² vane at the back. The head should balance near the yaw sleeve.

Build the dump-load controller from the circuit in the notes. Set it with an adjustable supply or a charged battery so the load switches on at 14.4V and off near 13.7V. Mount the MOSFET and rectifier on the heatsink.
steps.warn: Dump loads get very hot. Mount bulbs or resistors on metal, away from anything that burns.

steps.text: At the battery: fit the fuse within 30 cm of battery positive, then wire rectifier + → fuse → battery +, rectifier − → battery −. Connect the dump load and controller across the battery after the fuse. Wire the brake switch straight across the two motor leads, before the rectifier.
steps.warn: Remove rings and watches. A spanner across battery terminals can weld and burn you. Leave the fuse out until all wiring is done. Keep batteries ventilated: charging makes explosive hydrogen.

steps.text: Lay the tower on the ground with a hinge at the base. Fix guy cables at the top (and at mid-height on towers over 6 m) to four anchors placed at least half the tower height from the base. Rig a gin pole at the hinge to raise it.
Fit the head, run the cable down inside the tower, close the brake switch and tie a blade to the tower so the rotor cannot turn while you raise it.
Raise the tower slowly with a vehicle or second person on the gin-pole line, one person watching each side guy. Tension the guys evenly and check the tower is plumb from two directions.
steps.warn: Nobody stands in the fall zone: tower height plus rotor in every direction. Never climb a guyed pipe tower. Keep well clear of power lines.

steps.text: Untie the blade and open the brake. In wind, check the battery voltage rises and the dump load clicks on near 14.4V. If it never charges in a good wind, check the rectifier and the cut-in maths in the notes.
steps.warn: A spinning rotor can break bones or throw a blade. Brake it and wait for it to stop before touching anything.

steps.text: Every month and after storms: lower the tower, check blades for cracks, bolts and guys for tension, and untwist the down cable. Close the brake switch in a lull and lower the tower before forecast gales; this simple design has no furling.

notes:
## How it works
A treadmill motor is a permanent-magnet DC motor. Spin it and it makes DC, with voltage roughly proportional to speed. The rectifier stops the battery from driving the motor back and makes polarity not matter. The battery holds the voltage steady; the dump load burns off surplus once the battery is full, so the turbine always has a load and cannot overspeed.

## Power you can expect
Wind power = 0.5 × 1.2 × rotor area (m²) × wind speed³ (m/s) × efficiency. Home-made PVC rotors driving a battery-clamped brushed motor manage about 0.10–0.20 overall.

| Rotor | 4 m/s | 6 m/s | 8 m/s | 10 m/s | 12 m/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.2 m | 4–9W | 15–30W | 35–70W | 70–135W | 115–235W |
| 1.5 m | 7–14W | 25–45W | 55–110W | 105–210W | 185–365W |
| 1.8 m | 10–20W | 35–65W | 80–155W | 155–305W | 265–530W |

These are ceilings. Output is zero until the rotor is fast enough to beat battery voltage (cut-in), so light-wind figures are often not reached. Three 600–750 mm blades on a 200 mm hub give a rotor of about 1.4–1.7 m.

## Cut-in maths
- Rotor rpm ≈ tip-speed ratio × wind (m/s) × 60 ÷ (π × diameter in m). PVC blades run at a tip-speed ratio of about 4–5.
- Cut-in rpm ≈ (battery V + 1.4V rectifier drop) ÷ (volts per rpm).
- Example: motor at 19V per 1,000 rpm → cut-in about 760 rpm. A 1.2 m rotor at TSR 5 reaches that at about 9.5 m/s: too windy to be useful. A motor at 36V per 1,000 rpm cuts in at about 400 rpm, about 5 m/s on the same rotor.
- If your motor is low on volts per rpm, use a smaller rotor (faster spin), run a 6V battery, or add a belt step-up. A 24V battery needs twice the rpm.

## Wire size
Voltage drop = current × 2 × one-way length × ohms per metre. Keep it under 5% (0.6V at 12V).
- 10 AWG (6 mm²): about 3.3 mΩ/m. 6 AWG (16 mm²): about 1.3 mΩ/m.
- At 15A, 10 AWG is fine to about 6 m one way; 6 AWG to about 15 m.
- Put the battery near the tower base and run the loads' wiring from there.

## Fuse
The fuse protects the cable from the battery. Rate it a little above the turbine's peak current (300W ÷ 12V ≈ 25A → 30–40A fuse) and below the cable's rating.

## Dump-load controller (TL431 trigger)
- Divider: 47 kΩ (top, use 39 kΩ plus a 10 kΩ trimmer) from battery + to the TL431 reference pin, 10 kΩ from reference to battery −. Trip voltage ≈ 2.5 × (1 + top ÷ bottom).
- TL431 anode to −. Cathode → 1 kΩ → PNP base. 10 kΩ from PNP base to PNP emitter. PNP emitter to battery +.
- PNP collector → 1 kΩ → MOSFET gate, with 10 kΩ from gate to −.
- MOSFET drain to the dump load's lower end, source to −. Dump load upper end to battery + (after the fuse).
- Hysteresis: about 1 MΩ from the PNP collector back to the TL431 reference pin. This gives roughly on at 14.4V, off at 13.7V.
- Check on a bench supply before trusting it. Halogen bulbs draw several times their rated current for an instant when cold; use a MOSFET rated at least 2–3× the bulbs' running current, or power resistors, which have no surge.

## Variations
- Direct-drive washing-machine motors (outer-rotor brushless) make power at lower rpm. They give 3-phase AC: use a 3-phase rectifier or three bridge rectifiers.
- Car alternators need 1,000+ rpm and draw field current: poor for small wind.
- A 24V system halves current and cable size, but needs double the cut-in speed.

## Troubleshooting
- Spins but no current: below cut-in, rectifier open, or fuse blown. Measure open-circuit volts at the motor.
- Turns slowly even in strong wind: blades on backwards (hollow side should face the wind) or the brake switch half on.
- Shakes the tower: rotor out of balance or a blade cracked.
- Battery boils: dump load not switching. Lower the turbine until it works.

## If you lack a part
- No rectifier: use the diodes from a car alternator's rectifier pack, or a large Schottky from a PC power supply (60V or more).
- No controller: switch the dump load by hand when the battery reads over 14.4V, and brake the turbine whenever nobody is watching.
- No PVC: carve blades from straight-grained wood, or cut them from a plastic drum. Balance matters more than shape.
